newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa markets cheer disciplined budget.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa markets cheer disciplined budget.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel announced the next steps in the easing of exchange controls in an investor-friendly maiden budget on Wednesday, cheering the rand and government bonds.

Delivering on a long-standing promise to narrow the gap between state income and expenditure, he estimated the budget deficit in the year to March 31, 1998, at 24.7 billion rand or four percent of gross domestic product, down from 5.1 percent.

The combination of a relaxation in capital controls and a disciplined budget, including severe expenditure cuts, was welcomed by markets that have been wary of Manuel since he took over from former banker Chris Liebenberg just under a year ago.
"It seems to be an investor-friendly budget," said Dave Sadler, chief foreign exchange dealer at First National Bank in Johannesburg, as the rand gained two cents against the dollar to stand at 4.41.
Bond yields fell about 20 basis points on the day, with traders bullish about Manuel's budget.
Manuel left value added tax unchanged at 14 percent, cut personal tax by 2.8 billion rand, granted limited relief to companies and investors, and halved the tax on share dealing.
But the budget was dominated by the announcement of measures to relax remaining exchange controls on South African nationals and residents.

"It is from our perspective a philosophical shift from a situation that has been essentially controlled, with a few exceptions, to one that is essentially free, with a few exceptions," he told a pre-budget news conference.
Manuel said individuals would be able to invest a limited amount directly abroad or hold foreign currency deposits with South African banks.
South African nationals and residents would for the first time be free to keep funds earned abroad outside the country.
The move will take effect from July 1 and specific ceilings will be announced before then.
Manuel said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television later that the personal investment allowance would be well over 80,000 rand.
Companies will also be given increased freedom to invest overseas and will be able to raise foreign funding on the strength of their South Africa balance sheets.

"We move now to an environment in which South Africans can make ordinary transactions abroad freely, while the constraints which remain on large movements of capital will increasingly give way to procedural and prudential supervision," he said.
Manuel announced expenditure plans totalling 186.7 billion, up 6.1 percent on last year, but substantially lower than projected 8.5 percent inflation.
He estimated revenue, boosted by 2.5 billion from more efficient tax collection, but reduced by a 2.8 billion rand tax relief package, at 161.9 billion.
"This budget is a tough budget. It demands substantially more austerity from government than many of its forerunners have," Manuel told parliament in his budget address.
Analysts welcomed the tough line on spending, although Herman van Papendorp of SMK Securities said the expenditure target might prove hard to meet.

Despite the fiscal rigour of the budget, Manuel said the government had not sacrificed its plan to transform South Africa's once white-ruled society and said poverty relief was a key focus of spending.

He allocated 40 billion rand to education, 20 billion to health care, 18 billion to welfare and four billion to housing. In a renewed assault on escalating crime, almost 30 billion rand was budgeted for police, defence, justice and prisons.
However, defence spending was down 667 million rand to 9.579 billion, the biggest loser, making way for more social spending.
"In this budget we make a substantial allocation to poverty relief. We invest in people through a significant reprioritisation of expenditures in favour of social development," Manuel said.
The budget will also ease the individual tax burden on people earning below 60,000 rand a year.
